sections.text: Sometimes, and it depends on why the number is low. If a low eGFR comes from a temporary cause, the number can come back up once the cause is dealt with. If it comes from long-lasting kidney damage, the NIDDK says advanced, long-lasting chronic kidney disease (CKD) typically cannot be reversed, and the CDC says CKD usually gets worse over time, though treatment has been shown to slow it. For most people with CKD, the realistic goal is therefore not a higher eGFR but a slower decline. This article lays out what the primary sources say, and where the evidence is thinner than headlines suggest.

This is general education, not medical advice. Do not start, stop or change any medicine, supplement, diet or fluid plan because of a web page. A nephrologist or your own clinician can interpret your eGFR alongside your urine albumin, blood pressure, other conditions and medicines.
Why an eGFR can move without the kidneys changing

eGFR is not measured directly. It is calculated from serum creatinine, age and sex. The 2021 CKD-EPI equation used by our GFR calculator is eGFR = 142 x min(SCr/k, 1)^a x max(SCr/k, 1)^-1.200 x 0.9938^age, multiplied by 1.012 for females, with k = 0.9 and a = -0.302 for males. Because creatinine sits inside the formula, anything that changes the creatinine value changes the result. The table holds a 55-year-old man constant and changes only creatinine (computed with that formula, rounded to one decimal).

Going from a creatinine of 1.3 to 1.8 lowers the estimate from 64.9 to 43.9, about a third. Our calculator's own documentation lists dehydration, recent strenuous exercise, some medicines and acute illness among the things that can temporarily affect a reading, and notes that the equation assumes steady-state kidney function, so it is unreliable during acute kidney injury or rapidly changing creatinine. That is why clinicians look at repeat results over time, and why a single low value should be repeated and discussed rather than acted on.
Blood pressure: the strongest lever, with a caveat

The NIDDK describes controlling blood pressure as the most important step in treating kidney disease. What target to aim for is less settled. The 2021 KDIGO guideline recommends a systolic target below 120 mm Hg, measured with a standardized office technique, for most adults with CKD who are not on dialysis (children and kidney transplant recipients are exceptions). The KDOQI US commentary on that guideline noted a weak evidence base, especially for people with diabetes and advanced CKD. The NIDDK's clinician page also cites a goal of below 140/90 mm Hg from an earlier guideline. Different bodies, different targets: yours should come from your clinician.

The trial behind the lower target is SPRINT. It enrolled 9,361 people with systolic pressure of 130 mm Hg or higher and increased cardiovascular risk but without diabetes, and compared a systolic target below 120 with one below 140. The primary cardiovascular outcome occurred at 1.65 percent per year versus 2.19 percent per year (hazard ratio 0.75). That is a cardiovascular result. For kidney outcomes the picture was different. In the 2,646 participants who had CKD at the start (about 1,330 intensive, 1,316 standard), the kidney composite of a 50 percent or greater eGFR drop or kidney failure occurred in 15 versus 16 people (hazard ratio 0.90, 95 percent confidence interval 0.44 to 1.83), which is no demonstrated difference. After the first six months, eGFR fell slightly faster in the intensive group (0.47 versus 0.32 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year). The main trial also reported acute kidney injury in 4.1 percent of the intensive group versus 2.5 percent of the standard group. A claim that intensive control cuts kidney outcomes by some neat percentage is not what these trial reports show.

Diabetes is a major risk factor for CKD, and the NIDDK says optimal glucose control may reduce the risk of developing albuminuria. The classic evidence is UKPDS 33, which followed 3,867 people with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes for about ten years. Median HbA1c was 7.0 percent with intensive therapy versus 7.9 percent with conventional therapy. Microvascular endpoints were 25 percent lower (95 percent confidence interval 7 to 40), and any diabetes-related endpoint was 12 percent lower. Two cautions: the microvascular figure is a combined outcome, not a kidney-only result, and intensive treatment also brought more hypoglycaemic episodes and about 2.9 kg of average weight gain. HbA1c goals are individualized, and the CDC advises people with diabetes to have A1C tested at least twice a year.

items: Smoking. The NIDDK links cigarette smoking with abnormal urine albumin and with CKD progression, and the CDC advises quitting as soon as possible. No reliable single percentage is attached to this here.

Weight and activity. The CDC advises losing weight if you have overweight or obesity, and the NIDDK suggests being active for 30 minutes or more on most days, adjusted to what your clinician says is safe for you.

Over-the-counter pain relievers and supplements. The NIDDK warns that NSAIDs can damage the kidneys and lead to acute kidney injury, especially in people with kidney disease, and advises asking a pharmacist how supplements may affect your kidneys. Check before taking anything new.

Prescribed medicines. The NIDDK says two classes of blood pressure medicine may slow kidney disease and delay kidney failure, and larger trials have tested newer classes in CKD. Whether any of these suits you depends on your labs and other conditions. That decision belongs to your nephrologist, and the CDC's advice is simply to take medicines as prescribed.

Diet. Targets for sodium, protein, potassium and phosphorus vary by stage and test results, so see our kidney-friendly diet guide and work with a renal dietitian rather than copying a number from the internet.

sections.text: Worked example: what a slower decline is worth

To see why slowing decline matters, assume someone starts at an eGFR of 45 and loses a constant amount each year. The rates below are illustrative assumptions, not predictions or targets, and real trends are rarely a straight line. Years to reach 15 is (45 minus 15) divided by the yearly loss.

The same starting point leads to very different timelines, which is the real meaning of a treatment working: the slope flattens even though the number does not climb. Part of any decline is simply age. In the equation, each extra year multiplies eGFR by 0.9938, about 0.6 percent, so ten extra years at an unchanged creatinine lowers the estimate by about 6 percent (0.9938 to the 10th power is 0.940).

items: Reacting to one reading. Repeat tests and the trend matter more, and CKD staging also uses a urine albumin test. The NKF recommends two tests, eGFR and uACR.

Chasing a higher number with cleanses, teas or supplements. None of the NIDDK, NKF or CDC sources used here describes a product that reverses CKD, and some supplements can affect the kidneys or interact with medicines.
Treating a creatinine-based estimate as exact. It is less reliable at extremes of muscle mass and during rapid change, and a cystatin C test is sometimes used to confirm.
Waiting for symptoms. The NKF notes CKD often has no symptoms early, and the CDC estimates more than 1 in 7 US adults have CKD, with as many as 9 in 10 not knowing it.

sections.heading: Track Your GFR Over Time
sections.body: Use our free GFR calculator to see how a creatinine value translates to eGFR with the 2021 CKD-EPI equation, then discuss the trend with your clinician.
